title: Conversational executor: safe result injection, chain fallbacks, and recursion limits
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Add safeguards and compatibility layers to the core tool execution loop used by streaming chat and function-calling flows. The change set covers: deterministic result injection semantics, guarded multi-tool chaining with fallback policies, recursion/loop detection with soft/hard limits, and compatibility adapters for v1/v2 API clients. This ticket ties into the broader initiative to make function/tool calling reliable for production conversational agents and to ensure streaming responses remain consistent when tools produce late-arriving outputs.
background: We currently support tool/function calling and streaming tokens, but there are recurring incidents and integration gaps: 1) tool outputs injected mid-stream cause partial structured outputs that downstream parsers mis-handle, 2) user-defined tools can indirectly trigger other tools creating recursion loops, and 3) older API clients expect a synchronous invocation model and brittle contracts. Recent customer reports and internal postmortems (INC-2025-07) showed confusion when streaming chat resumed after a tool returned, producing duplicate JSON fragments and broken structured outputs.
goals: Define canonical semantics for result injection into streaming responses (atomic boundaries + resume markers)
Implement recursion/loop guards with configurable soft (warnings) and hard (abort) thresholds
Support chained tool pipelines with deterministic fallback policies (model variant, no-tool fallback)
Provide compatibility adapter that accepts legacy sync-style client expectations and maps them to streaming behavior
non_goals: Rewriting the entire orchestration layer — this is iterative, focused on the executor loop
Changing model-level decoding strategies beyond what is required to support injection semantics
acceptance_criteria: When a tool is invoked during a streaming response, injected content is enclosed by explicit resume markers and a single atomic JSON payload is emitted (no partial JSON fragments are allowed)

System detects recursion after N tool invocations within a single request (default N=5) and applies configured policy: warn -> attempt compact fallback -> abort with structured error if hard limit reached
A fallback policy can be attached to an endpoint: preferred-model -> smaller-quantized-variant -> no-tool-safe-mode. The executor implements policy selection deterministically under load
Legacy clients opting into compatibility mode receive a single completed response (blocking) that preserves structured outputs, with a server-side streaming-to-blocking adapter
Unit + integration tests cover streaming + tool injection + parser recovery scenarios; end-to-end test against sample legacy client
implementation_notes: Introduce InjectionFrame markers in the stream: [INJECT_BEGIN id=<uuid> meta={...}] and [INJECT_END id=<uuid>] (these are stripped for blocking responses)
Executor must append provenance headers to injected tool payloads: tool_id, tool_version, elapsed_ms
Maintain a per-request ToolInvocationStack with lightweight canonical fingerprints (tool_id + input_hash). Track depth and detect repeats for loop heuristics
Provide two configuration surfaces: endpoint-level policy config and runtime global defaults. Policy fields: max_invocations, soft_threshold_pct, fallback_sequence, allow_nested_tools
Compatibility adapter: detect header X-Redwood-Legacy-Client=true and buffer streaming frames until INJECT_END for each injected block, then return a single aggregated payload
Ensure streaming transport (HTTP/2 SSE and websocket) preserves frame boundaries for injection markers; update SDKs to expose injected frames to consumers that want raw access
Add metrics: tools.invocations.total, tools.recursion.detected, tools.injection.partial_frames, streaming.resume_latency, executor.fallback.engaged
progress_updates: 2026-03-01: Kickoff meeting. Agreed on InjectionFrame markers and basic stack fingerprint approach

2026-03-03: Spike implemented in runtime branch feature/exec-injection-spike. Prototype demonstrates resume markers in SSE and websocket clients. POC PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-runtime/pull/4123

2026-03-06: Design review with API and SDK teams. Decision: default max_invocations=5, soft threshold triggers a 'compact' fallback that replaces tool output with a short summary generated by a secondary model
2026-03-09: Began implementation of ToolInvocationStack and metrics. Integration tests drafted for streaming + injection scenarios
2026-03-10: Marking initial server-side implementation as feature-flagged behind runtime.config.exec_injection=true for canary rollout
comments: PM review (Rina Chen 2026-03-04): Make sure customer-visible errors are stable and documented in the API changelog
Design feedback (Jules Martin 2026-03-05): Consider edge case where tool returns another tool invocation request — prefer abort over unbounded nesting
Security (Leah Ortiz 2026-03-07): Add requirement to sanitize tool outputs before injection to reduce prompt-injection risk; mark for security review
SDK lead (Omar Singh 2026-03-08): We'll need an SDK flag to surface raw injection markers for advanced users; default will hide markers and present merged content
tests: Unit: InjectionFrame parsing and strip/aggregate logic
Integration: SSE & Websocket streaming with single-tool and chained-tool scenarios
E2E: Legacy client mode where streaming-to-blocking adapter must return a single well-formed JSON response
Chaos: Simulate delayed tool responses and ensure resume markers and timeouts behave as expected
rollout_plan: Canary deploy to 5% of traffic for low-latency endpoints for 72 hours
Observe metrics tools.injection.partial_frames and streaming.resume_latency, rollback threshold if >2x baseline errors
If stable, expand to 25% for 48 hours, then full rollout and remove flag after 2 weeks of stability
Publish API changelog and SDK updates, call out backwards-compatible legacy header behavior
